title: test-0064-SOC-HIS-CRAFTS
passage: Many people mistakenly believe that Indian handloom weaving vanished instantly when British machine-made cloth arrived, or that the decline of Indian iron smelting was due to a lack of natural resources. In reality, Indian textiles remained globally popular for centuries because of their fine quality. The term 'Calico' actually comes from Calicut in India, where Portuguese traders first encountered cotton textiles, not from California. While British industrialization introduced machines like the Spinning Jenny—an invention that automated spinning rather than a person—Indian weavers did not simply stop working. Many survived by producing specialized cloth that machines could not easily replicate. Similarly, the decline of traditional iron smelting was not caused by a shortage of iron ore, but by strict colonial forest laws that restricted access to charcoal. When the Tata Iron and Steel Company (TISCO) began production in 1912, it was built in the village of Sakchi, which later became Jamshedpur. This modern industry actually expanded during World War I, as the British needed steel for war supplies, proving that the industry was resilient rather than doomed by global conflict.
